title: Polynomial-time robust spectral estimation
formal: For every fixed \(q\in[2,\infty]\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that always recovers a robust low-rank representation of an unknown clean matrix from bounded perturbations to every data point, with the spectral-error guarantee available information-theoretically in Proposition 27? Specifically, do there exist, for each fixed \(q\), a uniform algorithm \(\mathcal A_q\) and constants \(b_q,C_q,B_q,a_q\ge1\) such that the following holds for all integers \(n,m\ge1\), \(0\le r\le n\), real \(\kappa,\delta\ge0\), and matrices \(A,\widetilde A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) satisfying \(\|\widetilde A_j-A_j\|_q\le\delta\) for every column \(j\)? Given only \((\widetilde A,r,\kappa,\delta)\), the algorithm must output an orthogonal projection \(\widehat\Pi\) with \[\operatorname{rank}(\widehat\Pi)\le r,\qquad \|\widehat\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le b_q\kappa,\] and, for every \(\eta>0\), \[\|(I_n-\widehat\Pi)A\|_{2\to2}\le C_q(1+\eta^{-1})\left(\operatorname{OPT}_{q,r,\kappa}(A)+\sqrt m\,\delta\kappa\right)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,\|A\|_{2\to2}.\] The same output must satisfy every \(\eta\); \(\eta\) is an analysis parameter, not an extra source of clean-data information. Require at most \(B_q(n+m+1)^{a_q}\) operations in the explicit fixed-\(q\) real-arithmetic model below. The output must be a projection, even when the observed matrix has large spectral distortion; reporting only that the input was poisoned is insufficient.

source_formulation.text: Can a polynomial-time estimator always return a robust low-rank projection with the spectral-error guarantee available information-theoretically under bounded perturbations to every training point?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: A representation can be stable against future perturbations and still be difficult to learn from already corrupted data. This question asks whether worst-case robust spectral reconstruction is computationally attainable whenever it is information-theoretically possible. It isolates a gap that is hidden if an algorithm may simply report severe corruption.
status_note: The 2021 source’s Proposition 27 gives the information-theoretic spectral recovery guarantee, while its efficient Theorem 25 may return a poisoning certificate. The exact always-return-a-projection target, rank bound, robustness factor and eta tradeoff are retained. Related Gaussian principal-subspace results have extra distributional structure. The live original manuscript history and bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 did not yield a verified theorem resolving this full worst-case question. Status is uncertain, not a proof of openness. Polynomial time is explicitly interpreted in a fixed-q exact-real arithmetic model with unit-cost q-powers; neither finite-bit equivalence nor an unrestricted norm/optimization oracle is asserted.

importance.reason: A concrete computational gap for robust dimension reduction, separating guaranteed reconstruction from certification under perturbations affecting every data point.

sentences: The card asks for polynomial-time recovery of a robust low-rank representation when every training point may have been adversarially perturbed.
The output must approximate the unknown clean matrix in spectral norm while respecting the rank budget and induced-norm robustness bound.
The source proves that such recovery is information-theoretically possible but its efficient spectral method may only certify severe poisoning.
The statement preserves the full range of fixed norm exponents and the same-output error tradeoff in an explicit real-arithmetic model.
A Lean resolution must prove or refute guaranteed recovery with the stated approximation and computational costs, without extra distributional assumptions.

definitions:
Columns \(A_j\in\mathbb R^n\) are the clean data points and columns \(\widetilde A_j\) are the supplied observations. An adversary may change every column, in any correlated way, subject only to the displayed per-column constraint. There is no distributional assumption, random design, fraction of uncontaminated points, spectral gap, incoherence or sparsity promise. For finite \(q\), \(\|v\|_q=(\sum_i|v_i|^q)^{1/q}\); for \(q=\infty\), \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). Thus the infinite-norm version permits a change of magnitude at most \(\delta\) to every entry.

For a matrix \(M\), \(\|M\|_{u\to v}=\sup_{\|x\|_u\le1}\|Mx\|_v\), with input and output dimensions determined by \(M\). The spectral norm \(\|M\|_{2\to2}\) is its largest singular value; it measures maximum Euclidean amplification, not the sum of squared entry errors. A real \(n\times n\) matrix \(\Pi\) is an orthogonal projection when \(\Pi^T=\Pi\) and \(\Pi^2=\Pi\). Its rank is the dimension of its range. The condition \(\|\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le\kappa\) means every input perturbation of \(q\)-norm at most \(\delta\) moves the projected point by at most \(\kappa\delta\) in Euclidean norm.

Define the clean benchmark by \[\operatorname{OPT}_{q,r,\kappa}(A)=\min\{\|(I_n-\Pi)A\|_{2\to2}:\Pi^T=\Pi=\Pi^2,\ \operatorname{rank}(\Pi)\le r,\ \|\Pi\|_{q\to2}\le\kappa\}.\] The zero projection is feasible, so the class is nonempty; it is a closed bounded subset of the finite-dimensional matrix space and the minimum exists. The rank constraint is an upper bound, as in the source’s robust approximation framework and Theorem 25. The algorithm is not given the optimizer, its value, the clean matrix, its norm or the perturbation matrix. Only \(n,m\), the observed entries, rank budget and two corruption/robustness bounds are available. The output is the complete \(n\times n\) projection matrix. No extra data access is available at evaluation.

The constants \(b_q,C_q,B_q,a_q\) may depend on the fixed norm exponent, consistently with the source’s \(q\)-dependent approximation constants, but not on dimensions, rank, matrix entries, \(\kappa,\delta\) or \(\eta\). For a fixed \(q\), the same finite algorithm works on all sizes. The recovery inequality is the source’s constant-factor spectral guarantee with its additive corruption term and \(\eta\)-tradeoff, not an exact recovery or squared-Frobenius guarantee. It is valid for every compatible clean matrix \(A\): the algorithm sees only \(\widetilde A\). In particular, \(\eta\) is universally quantified after the output; a different projection for each value is not silently substituted.

Computational convention: the observed matrix and real bounds are held in exact real registers. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\) with a zero-denominator guard, comparisons, branching, square roots of nonnegative reals, discrete control and register access each cost one unit. For finite fixed \(q\), the primitives \(x\mapsto x^q\) and \(x\mapsto x^{1/q}\) on \(x\ge0\) also have unit cost, with \(0^q=0\). For \(q=\infty\), maxima and absolute values use comparisons instead. These are explicit elementary-power conventions for each fixed real \(q\), including exponents that are not rational; no algorithm uniform in an encoded variable exponent is requested. Program constants otherwise are rational. Reading each observed entry and writing each output entry costs one unit. The stated bound is a worst-case arithmetic-operation bound on every input, and the algorithm must always return a valid output satisfying the guarantees. It has no optimization oracle, spectral-decomposition oracle, induced-norm oracle, digit-extraction operation, clean-data oracle or general-real decision oracle. The norms used in the target are mathematical definitions, not free computational queries.

The source formulates its algorithms on real matrices and does not fix an entry-bit or approximation budget. The displayed model is an explicit real-arithmetic interpretation of polynomial time; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity formulation. In particular, exact real output and the special fixed-\(q\) power operations must not be imported into a finite-bit claim without a separate numerical analysis. The full range of fixed exponents, including infinity, is preserved rather than restricting the question to the illustrative entrywise case.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the displayed existence statement for every fixed \(q\), or of its negation. An affirmative answer must construct the uniform algorithms, prove their polynomial arithmetic costs, exact projection/rank properties, constant-factor robustness and clean spectral-error bounds for every adversarially compatible input and every \(\eta>0\). A negative answer must exhibit an exponent for which no algorithm and constants with these guarantees exist; a lower bound for one heuristic is insufficient. A conditional complexity assumption must remain a hypothesis unless established. Returning a corruption certificate, controlling Frobenius error alone, allowing a larger rank, assuming Gaussian/spiked input, or giving an inefficient estimator does not meet the stated goal. The objective is the explicit approximation inequality, so a numerical eigenvector estimate without a proved error and robustness bound does not constitute a resolution.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis minimizes reconstruction error without a robustness constraint. Here the projection must also limit how much a small change to one point can move its representation. Training data may already be corrupted, so the reconstruction guarantee concerns an unknown matrix rather than the observed matrix alone.

The source proves efficient recovery with Frobenius error and gives a different spectral algorithm that may return a certificate of substantial poisoning. Proposition 27 establishes that a robust projection satisfying the stronger spectral guarantee exists information-theoretically. The selected open question asks for efficient recovery with that guarantee, without the certification-only alternative.

The rank bound and robustness factor are separate requirements. The source’s worst-case spectral approximation theorem also has a variant trading increased rank for improved approximation, but that enlarged-rank variant does not by itself give the rank-at-most-r recovery requested here.

The additive term involving column count, corruption size and robustness is essential to the target. Small changes to all coordinates can collectively create a large matrix perturbation, so controlling each point is different from assuming the whole perturbation has small spectral norm.

The related COLT 2020 work studies principal-subspace estimation for Gaussian covariance models under per-sample adversarial perturbations. Its statistical assumptions supply structure absent from an arbitrary clean matrix. The 2021 source explicitly distinguishes that setting from its worst-case recovery question.

The live arXiv history lists a last revision in August 2021. Bounded later-work searches did not locate a checked theorem matching the full always-recover spectral interface; that search outcome is not a proof of openness. The card therefore keeps uncertain current status and states its computational convention explicitly.
